chapter.title: Walking the site: reading what got built

cards.body: Open the folder of any small web app and you'll find a handful of files with names like index.html. Only 4 kinds do the real work, and they map onto a house: **the page is the rooms, the styling is the paint, the logic is the wiring, and the settings are the permit folder**. Walk the site once and you'll know which door to knock on when something looks off.
cards.simpler: Open the folder of any small web app and you'll see a handful of files. Only 4 kinds matter, and they match the parts of a house: **the page is the rooms, the styling is the paint, the logic is the wiring, and the settings are the permit folder**. Once you've walked the site once, you'll know which door to knock on when something looks wrong.

cards.prompt: Your builder finished the kitchen. It works, but every cupboard is painted lime green. In the house picture, which kind of file holds the lime green?

options.text: The page: the rooms and what's in them
The styling: the paint, fonts and spacing
The logic: the wiring that makes things happen

whyNot.a: That's the page, not the styling: the page says a cupboard exists, not what colour it is.
whyNot.c: That's the logic, not the styling: wiring decides what happens when you press something, not how it looks.

cards.reteach: Think of the 4 files as 4 trades on one house. The page lays out rooms and fittings. The styling paints and decorates. Colour is a paint job, so it lives in the styling file.

cards.title: Rooms and paint
cards.body:
Two of the four files decide what you see.

The *page file*, usually named index.html, is the rooms and the fittings: a heading here, a button there, a box to type in. HTML is just the name of the language for listing what's on a page. If a button exists at all, it's because this file says so.

The *styling file*, usually ending in .css, is the paint, the fonts and the spacing. **The page says what exists; the styling says how it looks.** Change one line in it and a grey button turns blue, like swapping a tin of paint.
cards.simpler:
Two of the four files decide what you see.

The page file, usually named index.html, is the rooms and fittings. A heading, a button, a box to type in. HTML is just the name of the language that lists what's on a page. If a button exists, it's because this file says so.

The styling file, usually ending in .css, is the paint, the fonts and the spacing. **The page says what exists; the styling says how it looks.** Change one line and a grey button turns blue, like opening a new tin of paint.

cards.title: Sam and the lime green button
cards.body: Sam asks Claude Code for a tip calculator. The folder comes back with 4 files: index.html, style.css, app.js and package.json. The Calculate button is lime green, which was nobody's plan. Sam opens style.css, searches for 'green', and finds one line: background: lime. **One word in the styling file, one lime button.** Sam types 'change the button to dark blue' and watches that single line change instead of the whole house.
cards.simpler: Sam asks Claude Code for a tip calculator. Four files come back: index.html, style.css, app.js and package.json. The Calculate button is lime green. Nobody wanted that. Sam opens style.css, searches for 'green', and finds one line: background: lime. **One word in the styling file, one lime button.** Sam types 'change the button to dark blue' and watches that single line change. The rest of the house stays as it was.

cards.prompt: Same app. Now the Calculate button looks perfect but does nothing when Sam clicks it. Which file do you ask Claude to look at?

whyNot.a: That's the page, not the logic: the page proves the button exists, and it does. What's missing is what happens on the click.
whyNot.b: That's the styling, not the logic: paint can make a button pretty, but paint never makes a switch work.

cards.reteach: A button that looks right but does nothing is a wiring problem. The logic file holds the instructions for what happens when something is pressed. Ask Claude to look there.

cards.title: Wiring and the permit folder
cards.body:
The *logic file*, usually ending in .js, is the wiring. JavaScript is the language that says what happens when a button is pressed or a number is typed. The page can have a perfect switch on the wall. Without this file, nothing lights up.

The *settings file*, usually package.json, is the permit folder: the project's name, the tools it uses, and the command that starts it. You'd think it's where the action is. It isn't. It's paperwork, and you rarely touch it yourself.

**You don't need to read any of them line by line.** Ask Claude: 'Explain app.js in 5 plain sentences, no code.'
cards.simpler:
The logic file, usually ending in .js, is the wiring. JavaScript is the language that says what happens when you press a button or type a number. The page can have a perfect switch on the wall. Without this file, nothing lights up.

The settings file, usually package.json, is the permit folder. It holds the project's name, the tools it uses, and the command that starts it. It looks important. It's paperwork, and you rarely touch it.

**You don't need to read any of them line by line.** Ask Claude: 'Explain app.js in 5 plain sentences, no code.'

cards.body: Dev opens app.js, sees 180 lines of brackets, and closes the laptop with the feeling that coding isn't for them. The mistake was reading like a builder instead of asking like an owner. **You spot it when you've stared at a file for 2 minutes and haven't asked Claude a single question.** The fix is one line: 'What does this file do, in plain words?'
cards.simpler: Dev opens app.js, sees 180 lines of brackets, and shuts the laptop feeling that coding isn't for them. The mistake was reading like a builder instead of asking like an owner. An owner doesn't inspect the wiring. They ask the electrician what it does. **You spot it when you've stared at a file for 2 minutes and haven't asked Claude a single question.** The fix is one line: 'What does this file do, in plain words?'

cards.prompt: Claude finishes a job and says: 'I updated package.json to add the start command.' Which part of the house just changed?

options.text: The rooms: something new appeared on the page
The permit folder: the project's settings and tools

whyNot.a: That's the page, not the settings: nothing new shows up on screen when package.json changes.
whyNot.c: That's the styling, not the settings: package.json has no say in colours or fonts.

cards.reteach: package.json is the paperwork file. It records the project's name, its tools, and how to start it. Changes there alter how the project runs, not how it looks or what's on the page.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
A small web app is 4 kinds of file: the page is the rooms, the styling is the paint, the logic is the wiring, and the settings are the permit folder. **You never have to read them raw**: name the file and ask Claude to explain it in plain words.

Tomorrow: that red error message was written for Claude, not you.
cards.simpler:
A small web app is 4 kinds of file. The page is the rooms, the styling is the paint, the logic is the wiring, and the settings are the permit folder. **You never have to read them raw.** Name the file and ask Claude to explain it in plain words, the way you'd ask a builder to talk you through a house instead of handing you the blueprints.

Tomorrow: that red error message was written for Claude, not you.

cards.body: Open your project folder from chapter 1 in Claude Code and type: 'Walk me through this folder. One plain-English line per file, which of the 4 jobs it does, no code.'
cards.simpler: Open the project folder you made in chapter 1 inside Claude Code. Then type this: 'Walk me through this folder. One plain-English line per file, which of the 4 jobs it does, no code.' Think of it as asking a guide to show you round the house, room by room. **You read the tour, not the files.** Notice how little you need to open yourself.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now open a project folder, say which of the 4 jobs each main file does, and ask Claude to explain any file in plain words.
